mustInclude: The broken items from the sketch map (swing chain, cracked slide, torn safety mat, broken lamp) and why each is dangerous
How the faults affect local families: children who use it daily, the kindergarten group, no safe nearby alternative
Suggestions for immediate action (e.g. fence off or close the dangerous items, fix the lamp) and longer-term action (replace equipment, regular inspections)
Credit (not required): using the unanswered report of 20 October to strengthen the request
genreFeatures: Formal letter: 'Dear Sir or Madam' or 'Dear District Officer' and 'Yours faithfully, Chris Wong'
A clear opening sentence stating the purpose of the letter (reporting faults and requesting repairs)
Short paragraphs: purpose – problems and dangers – effect on families – requests – polite close
A subject line is welcome but not required
taskRequirements.registerTone: Formal, polite and firm. The writer is concerned and should sound urgent, but must not be rude, sarcastic or emotional towards the officer.
pitfalls: Copying the notes from the map word for word or listing them without explaining the danger
Ignoring the third point and asking only 'please repair it quickly'
Writing a complaint about the government in general rather than a request about this playground
Informal or wrong salutation and close ('Dear District Office', 'Hi', 'Best wishes', 'Yours sincerely' after 'Dear Sir or Madam')
Mentioning items that are working (fountain, benches) as problems, or inventing facts that contradict the map
Exaggerated claims ('children always fall down') that weaken credibility

content.high: Uses all four faults selectively, explaining the specific risk of each; refers to the kindergarten and the distant alternative, and may strengthen the request with the unanswered report; gives clear immediate and longer-term requests.
content.mid: Covers most faults and some effects on families, but explanations of danger are brief and the suggestions are general (repair everything) or miss one time frame.
content.low: Lists some faults with little or no explanation; effects are emotional rather than specific; suggestions missing or limited to 'repair quickly'; may misread the map.

language.high: Accurate, varied sentences; precise vocabulary for describing faults (snapped, cracked, torn, fenced off); consistently polite formal tone.
language.mid: Simple sentences mostly accurate; errors with passives, agreement and prepositions (complain the playground); occasional comma splices; register mostly appropriate.
language.low: Frequent errors in verb forms and agreement; vocabulary limited and often lifted from the notes; register slips (Dear District Office, Best wishes).

organisation.high: Purpose stated at once; logical paragraphs that move from problems to effects to requests; smooth linking; correct letter format.
organisation.mid: Clear paragraphs following the order of the map; cohesion relies on Firstly / Secondly / Moreover; format mostly correct.
organisation.low: Paragraphs loosely defined; ideas jump between problems and feelings; few linking devices; format errors.

bandGuide.notes: Any reasonable date for the letter is accepted. Candidates may say they are writing on behalf of other residents. Extra problems not on the map should not be credited if they contradict it. Mentioning the unanswered 20 October report is credited but not required: do not withhold marks if all three bullet points are fully covered.

mustInclude: A clear position (agreeing or disagreeing with the parent) on whether matches for students under 15 should stop keeping scores, held throughout the letter
Reference to the parent's letter (what it argued) as the reason for writing
At least two or three developed reasons, supported by examples (personal experience in school sport is welcome)
A response to the parent's reason (the pressure to win spoils the fun), either as a rebuttal (if disagreeing) or as support (if agreeing)
genreFeatures: Letter to the editor: 'Dear Editor' or 'Dear Sir or Madam' with 'Yours faithfully, Chris Wong' ('Yours sincerely' also accepted after 'Dear Editor')
Opening paragraph giving the context (the parent's letter) and the writer's stance
Body paragraphs each with one argument; a closing paragraph restating the view or making a call to readers
Written for newspaper readers, not as an essay or a speech
taskRequirements.registerTone: Formal to semi-formal and reasoned. Personal experience is welcome, but the writer should respect the parent's view and avoid lecturing readers.
pitfalls: Writing both sides ('advantages and disadvantages') instead of taking a stance
Drifting into whether students should do sport at all, or whether the government should build more sports grounds
Ignoring the age limit (under 15) or the parent's letter altogether
Opening with 'My name is Chris Wong' or copying the question as the first sentence
Circular arguments (scores are important because results matter) with no example
Overusing Moreover / Furthermore; using 'Best wishes' as the close

content.high: Firm, consistent stance; three well-developed reasons with concrete school-sport examples; engages directly with the parent's worry and offers a realistic alternative or response.
content.mid: Clear stance with relevant reasons, but examples are general and the reasons partly overlap; little engagement with the parent's point about pressure spoiling the fun.
content.low: Unclear or two-sided stance; ideas undeveloped or repeated; drifts into general benefits of sport or pressure on students.

language.high: Wide range of accurate structures; precise vocabulary for sport and argument (squad, fixtures, rebut); confident but courteous tone.
language.mid: Generally accurate simple sentences; errors in complex structures and typical local patterns (disagree this suggestion, due to it can, interested to watch).
language.low: Frequent errors in verb forms, word class and sentence structure; limited vocabulary; meaning sometimes unclear.

organisation.high: Clear introduction linking to the parent's letter; paragraphs build the case logically; concession and rebuttal handled smoothly; effective conclusion.
organisation.mid: Introduction, body and conclusion present; cohesion mechanical (Firstly, Secondly, Moreover, Furthermore); conclusion repeats the reasons.
organisation.low: Weak paragraphing; off-topic paragraph; little linking beyond 'And', 'But' and 'Also'.

bandGuide.notes: The question asks for one view: agreeing and disagreeing are both acceptable, but the stance must be clear. A brief concession is fine if the overall stance is clear; a two-sided 'advantages and disadvantages' answer only partly meets the task. Invented personal examples and match results are acceptable as support.

mustInclude: What the candidate would change in the school (two or three specific, realistic plans)
Why each change matters to students
Why students should vote for the speaker (credibility, experience, commitment) linked to the plans
A direct appeal for votes
genreFeatures: Speech: greeting the audience (e.g. 'Good afternoon, Principal, teachers and fellow students'), self-introduction
Spoken features: direct address (you, we), rhetorical questions, signposting for listeners
Clear closing appeal and 'Thank you'
No letter or essay format
taskRequirements.registerTone: Semi-formal, confident and friendly. The speaker addresses peers, so some warmth and humour suit, but the tone must stay respectful because the speech is given to the whole school, including teachers.
pitfalls: Unrealistic promises (no homework, change the uniform tomorrow) with no explanation of how
Spending most of the speech praising oneself with no plans, or listing plans with no reason to choose the speaker
Writing generally about what a Student Union is instead of the candidate's own platform
Essay-style conclusion ('In conclusion'), letter endings, or stock phrases such as 'Last but not least' and 'Thank you for your listening'
Overly casual or rude remarks about other candidates or teachers

content.high: Two or three specific, realistic proposals explained with concrete details of school life; credibility built through evidence or a plan for accountability; strong sense of the student audience.
content.mid: Relevant proposals with some reasons, but they are predictable (better canteen food, more activities) and the 'why vote for me' part is a list of qualities.
content.low: Vague or unrealistic promises; much self-praise or general talk about the Student Union; little sense of audience.

language.high: Varied, accurate sentences with effective spoken devices (direct address, rhetorical questions, short punchy sentences); natural, confident tone.
language.mid: Simple sentences generally accurate; errors in verb patterns (let students to have, vote me) and agreement; some stock phrases.
language.low: Frequent basic errors; very simple and repetitive vocabulary; tone too casual or flat.

organisation.high: Engaging opening, clearly signposted proposals, credible bridge to the appeal, memorable ending.
organisation.mid: Clear order (First of all, Secondly, Thirdly) but mechanical; the appeal for votes is tagged on at the end.
organisation.low: Ideas repeated or jump between topics; weak opening and ending.

bandGuide.notes: Candidates may invent their class, experience and school details. Proposals need not be large, but they should be explained. A greeting to students only is a minor register slip; do not penalise it heavily.

mustInclude: Benefits of running a small business as a secondary student (e.g. earning and managing money, practical skills such as pricing, record-keeping and dealing with customers, confidence), developed with examples
Risks or problems (e.g. less time for study and rest, losing money, buyers who do not pay, safety when meeting strangers, school rules or commitments to customers), developed with examples
Both sides discussed with reasonable balance; a personal view or practical advice for teenage readers (e.g. how to reduce the risks) is welcome but must not replace the discussion
Relevance to Hong Kong secondary students (e.g. school workload, tutorial classes, selling online from home)
genreFeatures: Magazine article: a title (and optional subheadings) suitable for a youth magazine
Engaging opening (a question, a scene or a classmate's example) rather than 'In this article, I will discuss…'
Direct address to teenage readers (you, we) where suitable
Ending that leaves readers with advice or a final thought; no letter format and no essay formula ('In conclusion')
taskRequirements.registerTone: Semi-formal and lively, written for teenage readers. Informative and balanced; friendly and practical rather than preachy.
pitfalls: Writing only about benefits or only about risks (the question asks for both)
Turning the article into a profile or interview of one successful student, or into a story
Drifting into part-time jobs for an employer (e.g. working in a restaurant) instead of running one's own business
Drifting into the general importance of money or what students can buy
Listing many benefits and risks without explaining or illustrating them
Essay features and stock phrases ('In conclusion', 'Every coin has two sides') or lecturing readers
Using real brand or platform names instead of general terms (online, social media)

content.high: Discusses both benefits and risks in depth with specific, believable examples from Hong Kong student life; weighs them sensibly and gives practical advice; strong sense of a teenage magazine audience.
content.mid: Covers both sides with relevant points, but examples are general, one side is thinner, and the ending repeats the points or gives general instructions.
content.low: Mainly one side, or points listed and repeated; drifts into part-time jobs or the general importance of money; little sense of audience.

language.high: Accurate, varied sentences; precise vocabulary for money and business (income, profit, costs, orders, customers); lively tone with natural direct address.
language.mid: Generally clear; errors in agreement, verb patterns and prepositions (let students to earn, ask money from, reply the customers); some repetitive phrasing.
language.low: Frequent errors in agreement, plurals, tense and word form; simple, repetitive vocabulary often lifted from the question; meaning occasionally unclear.

organisation.high: Engaging opening, clear sections on benefits, risks and advice (subheadings optional), smooth transitions, ending that leaves an impression.
organisation.mid: Clear paragraphs in a predictable order (introduction – benefits – risks – conclusion); mechanical linking (Firstly, Moreover, On the other hand); essay-like opening or ending.
organisation.low: Weak paragraphing; benefits and risks mixed or repeated; off-topic paragraph; essay-style ending.

bandGuide.notes: Candidates may use invented examples of themselves or classmates and invented figures. A conclusion favouring one side is acceptable if both benefits and risks are discussed. Part-time jobs for an employer are relevant only if linked to running one's own business.

mustInclude: The given sentence as the first sentence of the story
A plot that grows out of the notebook (what is inside it, what the narrator does about it)
Development of at least one character and some tension or turning point
A clear and satisfying ending that follows from the events
genreFeatures: Narrative in the past tense (the given sentence is past perfect)
Descriptive detail and dialogue where useful
A title is optional
Moral or lesson, if any, should arise from the story rather than be stated at length
taskRequirements.registerTone: Narrative and engaging, suitable for teenage readers; informal language in dialogue is acceptable.
pitfalls: Changing or omitting the given opening sentence
Shifting into the present tense after the first sentence
'It was all a dream' or other endings that cancel the plot
Listing events with no tension, description or character
Ending with a lecture ('From this experience, I learnt…') or 'This is my story. I hope you like it.'

content.high: Original, believable plot in which the notebook's contents matter; tension and a turning point; characters with clear feelings and motives; ending that resolves the story memorably.
content.mid: Coherent plot that follows from the notebook, but predictable; limited description; ending neat but rushed or followed by a stated moral.
content.low: Thin or confused plot; events not explained; weak or cancelled ending (dream); moralising.

language.high: Controlled past tenses; varied sentence lengths for effect; precise descriptive vocabulary; accurate dialogue punctuation.
language.mid: Mostly correct past tense with slips (conditionals, reported speech); simple descriptive vocabulary.
language.low: Tense switches throughout; frequent basic errors; very limited vocabulary.

organisation.high: Well-paced paragraphs; clear sequence with effective time shifts; ending linked back to the opening.
organisation.mid: Clear chronological paragraphs; simple time connectives (Next day, After that, Finally).

bandGuide.notes: Any setting and genre (realistic, mystery, humorous) is accepted. The story need not be set in Hong Kong.
